document.role: You are a scientific paper analyst specializing in dataset documentation and provenance.
document.task: Analyze the provided research paper and extract structured information about any new dataset(s) it introduces or makes available to the research community.

what_qualifies_as_a_new_dataset.qualifying_criteria: A paper qualifies as publishing a new dataset if it meets BOTH of the following: 1. Explicitly introduces, curates, collects, or constructs a novel dataset or benchmark. 2. Makes the dataset available publicly or upon request to the research community.
what_qualifies_as_a_new_dataset.evidence_signals: The following are signals that a qualifying dataset may exist in the paper: - Describes the dataset's size, format, collection methodology, or annotation process.
what_qualifies_as_a_new_dataset.does_not_qualify: A paper does NOT qualify if it: - Only uses existing datasets for experiments without releasing anything new. - Mentions a dataset incidentally without releasing it. - Describes internal/proprietary data with no public release path.

edge_cases.edge_case: A benchmark built entirely from curating pre-existing data qualifies, as long as the benchmark itself is newly introduced and released in this work.

A dataset counts as published by this paper only if it is introduced and released within this work. If the authors refer to a dataset they created in a prior publication — even using language like "we created" or "our dataset" — it does not necessarily qualify. Key signals that a dataset was released elsewhere include: a citation accompanying the dataset name, or the dataset being described without any release announcement or methodology description in this paper. Conversely, confirming signals that a dataset is introduced in this work include: explicit release language ("we release", "we publish", "available at"), a methodology or annotation section dedicated to the dataset, or the dataset listed among the paper's contributions.

Different splits (train/test/validation) of the same dataset should be captured as a single entry in `new_datasets`, reporting the total size across all splits. Different versions of the same dataset (e.g. v1 and v2) should be listed as separate entries.
If a paper extends a previously released dataset with new samples or annotations, treat it as a new dataset entry with the previous version listed as a source dataset.

If new data is collected directly from a primary source — such as an API (e.g. YouTube API, Twitter API), web scraping, sensors, human annotators, or any other first-hand collection method — this does NOT count as a source dataset and should NOT appear in `sources`. Treat it as original data creation and capture the collection method in `new_data_creation_method` instead.

document.where_to_look:
Look for the following types of content anywhere in the paper:
- Descriptions of how data was collected, annotated, or curated. - Statements about dataset size, format, or structure. - Explicit release announcements or mentions of a URL where the data can be accessed. - A list of contributions (typically in the abstract or introduction), which may name the dataset as a key contribution of the paper. - Data availability or author contribution statements, which often appear at the end of the paper or in footnotes. - Appendices, which frequently contain detailed dataset documentation, annotation guidelines, or data statements. - Descriptions of data used for experiments.
document.output_instructions:
- Respond in valid JSON only, with absolutely no text before or after. - If `publishes_new_dataset` is false, set `new_datasets` to an empty array []. - If a field's value cannot be determined from the paper, use null. Never use empty strings. - For `source_quote`, copy the relevant sentence(s) verbatim from the paper. If the evidence spans non-contiguous sentences, connect them with `[...]` to omit irrelevant text in between, such that a reader can understand the main evidence from the quote alone. - A dataset's `type` may be "original", "derived", or "mixed": - If a dataset is created by annotating or transforming existing data without creating any new data, set `type` to "derived" and `new_data_created` to false. This includes datasets that are remixes or aggregations of multiple existing datasets. - If a dataset is created by collecting or generating entirely new data, set `type` to "original" and `new_data_created` to true. - If a dataset combines newly created data with existing data, set `type` to "mixed" and `new_data_created` to true. - If a dataset's `type` is "original", set `sources` to an empty array []. - Pay close attention to dataset version information, as authors may refer to the same dataset inconsistently throughout the paper (e.g. using "ImageNet" and "ImageNet v2" interchangeably). Look for version numbers, year suffixes, or variant names across the full paper to identify the specific version(s) used. This applies to both newly introduced datasets and source datasets. If multiple versions of the same dataset are used, list each as a separate entry — in the `sources` array if they are source datasets, or as separate entries in `new_datasets` if they are newly introduced datasets. A strong signal that multiple versions are used is when the paper compares experimental results across different versions of the same dataset. - For source datasets, only report transformations or modifications in `filtering_and_transformation`. If data samples or annotations were used as-is, omit them. If nothing was changed, set this field to null. - A source dataset may be associated with multiple citations. Select the single most relevant paper using this priority order: 1. The paper that originally introduced or released the dataset (the "dataset paper"). 2. If no clear dataset paper exists, the paper most directly describing the dataset's content, size, or collection methodology. 3. If a specific version is identified, cite the paper that introduced that version rather than the original dataset paper. - Always populate `source_paper.relevance_reason`, regardless of which priority rule was applied. - For source dataset citations, authors do not always cite consistently. Before concluding that no citation exists for a source dataset, scan the entire paper — including all sections, footnotes, appendices, and captions — for any citation associated with that dataset name. If a citation is found anywhere in the paper, use it. - When a source dataset has no citation anywhere in the paper, determine which of the following cases applies and populate `source_paper` accordingly:
Case A — The dataset was published in this same paper: This applies when the source dataset is itself one of the new datasets introduced in this paper (i.e. it also appears in `new_datasets`). Generate a bibliographic string in APA format using available information from the paper (authors, year, title, venue). If insufficient information is available to generate a proper APA string, use "(self)" as the bibliographic string. Always populate `title` and `first_author` from the paper. Set `relevance_reason` to "Source dataset is published in the same paper."
Case B — The dataset was published in a sister paper: This applies when the dataset is associated with closely related work by overlapping authors (e.g. a companion paper, a concurrent preprint, or an earlier publication in the same research line) that is cited elsewhere in this paper. Identify the most relevant such citation and use it. Pay close attention to dataset version: if a specific version is used, cite the paper that introduced that version. Note that sister papers may share only some authors with the current paper.
Case C — Missing citation (likely an oversight): This applies when no citation can be found and the dataset does not appear to originate from this paper or a sister paper. Set `bibliographic_string`, `title`, and `first_author` to null. Set `relevance_reason` to "No citation provided."
document.output_schema: { "paper_title": "<full paper title>", "first_author_name": "<last, first — use the first name appearing in the author list>", "publishes_new_dataset": true | false, "new_datasets": [ { "name": "<dataset name, including version if identified>", "download_url": ["<url(s) to download the published dataset, as stated in the paper. Report all URLs if multiple are provided.>"], "domain": "<the research field of the dataset, e.g. NLP, computer vision, robotics. Use CS-centric terminology.>", "task": "<the specific task the dataset is designed for, e.g. question answering, object detection, speech recognition. If the dataset is general-purpose and not designed for a specific task, use null.>", "size": "<number of examples, images, tokens, hours, etc. Use whatever units are reported by the paper authors.>", "type": "original" | "derived" | "mixed", "new_data_created": true | false, "new_data_creation_method": "<if new_data_created is true: describe in 2-3 sentences how new data was obtained or generated, e.g. web scraping, crowdsourcing, sensors, diffusion model generation, LLM generation. Otherwise null.>", "annotation_method": "<if the authors performed new annotation as part of creating this dataset: describe in 2-3 sentences who annotated the data, what the annotation task involved, and any quality control measures reported. Annotations that already exist in a source dataset do not apply here. Otherwise null.>", "dataset_construction_summary": "<describe in 4-6 sentences a general summary of how the dataset was created, tying together data collection or generation, annotation, and processing into a coherent overview.>", "sources": [ { "source_dataset_name": "<name of the upstream source dataset, including version if identified>", "source_paper": { "bibliographic_string": "<the verbatim bibliographic string from the paper's reference list, if a citation exists. If no citation exists and the dataset was published in this same paper, generate an APA-format string from available information, or use \"(self)\" if insufficient information is available. If no citation exists and this appears to be a missing citation oversight, use null.>", "title": "<title of the source dataset paper. Always populate this field if the paper can be identified (whether cited, self-published, or a sister paper). Use null only when no citation exists and the source cannot be identified.>", "relevance_reason": "<one sentence explaining why this citation was chosen as most relevant — e.g. it is the original dataset paper, the most recent version, or the one explicitly named alongside the dataset. For datasets published in the same paper, use \"Source dataset is published in the same paper.\" For missing citations with no identifiable source, use \"No citation provided.\">" }, "source_quote": "<verbatim sentence(s) from the paper evidencing use of this source dataset. If the evidence spans non-contiguous sentences, connect them with [...].>", "filtering_and_transformation": "<describe in 2-3 sentences any filtering, sampling, cleaning, relabeling, augmentation, or other transformation applied to this source dataset's samples or annotations. Only report what was changed. If nothing was changed, set this to null.>" } ] } ] }
